When an operation's cost can scale with the full repository or dataset size, bound it to the actual work needed (e.g., diff against changed paths or local refs) instead of enumerating or fetching everything up front. Batch per-item work into a single call rather than spawning one subprocess or network round trip per item — for example, read many blobs with one `git cat-file --batch` call instead of one `git show` per file, which otherwise can flood the host with thousands of concurrent processes on large inputs. Never repeat work that has already been computed: reuse a result that was already fetched or produced (e.g., don't call an expensive capture function a second time just to get the value it already returned internally) instead of triggering a second costly round trip. Watch for per-item budgets/caps that multiply into an unbounded aggregate (a per-file cap times N files can blow past the intended total), and bound the aggregate explicitly. Dispose of any temporary files, caches, or buffers created to support these optimizations once they're no longer needed, rather than leaving them to accumulate indefinitely. Finally, validate performance-sensitive changes with real measurements (process counts, timing, memory) against representative data rather than relying solely on unit tests, since mocking subprocess/IO calls can hide the actual runtime behavior being optimized.
